src: Marks as of US close 4 Sep 2026. 502 daily bars, 44 relative-strength rows across a 45-symbol universe. Bid/ask unavailable on a weekend pull, so every price here is a close, a last or a settlement mark.

lede.h: August payrolls came in three times consensus and the long end repriced inside the hour
lede.s: Payrolls printed +162,000 against a consensus of 53,000, and July's previously reported loss of 23,000 was revised to a gain of 21,000. Unemployment held at 4.1%. Yields had been falling into the release and reversed hard: the 30Y finished at 5.24%, the 10Y at 4.77% after touching above 4.8%, the 2Y at 4.37%. Futures moved to better than even odds of a Fed hike this month. Next week's CPI and PPI now carry the decision.

lede.h: Crude gained about 9% on the week and energy equities did not follow it
lede.s: WTI sat near $91 on Friday, up roughly 21% over the month, on renewed US-Iran exchanges and thinning traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — six commodity vessels transited on Wednesday against a ten-day average near thirteen. US diesel reached its highest since mid-2022. Against that, XLE/USO fell 7.77% over four weeks and sits below its 50-day. Both legs are positive, so this is not a falling denominator: the commodity is simply running much faster than the companies that produce it.

lede.h: The regime read is CONFIRMED three-nil, and two of the three votes carry a failure inside them
lede.s: Equity internals votes fiscal dominance while failing its own independence test — the XBI-over-XLV spread at 1.77 does not pass, narrower than 2.19 a week ago but still short. Commodities votes fiscal dominance with a miner-beta flag set, which is the system saying the precious-metals move looks like equity beta rather than monetary demand. Only the rates family votes on unqualified evidence. A three-nil tally with one clean vote is a weaker reading than the number suggests.

lede.h: Correlation stood down rather than voting, and the two calibrations disagree
lede.s: The SPY/TLT 60-day correlation is 0.297976, which clears the full-history 95th percentile of 0.295643 but sits at only the 90.6th percentile against a trailing ten-year window whose own threshold is 0.354191. The family abstained on that disagreement. It rose from 0.291 last week, so it is warming toward the line rather than away from it, and it is not part of this week's three votes.

lede.h: Metals and crypto top the screen while decelerating hard
lede.s: IBIT +23.74, SIL +19.04 and GDX +18.07 are the three strongest four-week readings in the universe and all three are de-correlating from the index. But GDX has gone 26.10 → 18.07 and gold 8.45 → 4.18 over the week. Thirteen of forty-four rows fire the screen against nine a week ago, and the leaders are 17 to 19% above their own 50-day, so this describes where money has been rather than where it is going.

secNote: Ranked by RS_4wk, the actionable window. corr_shift is 20-day correlation to SPY minus 60-day: negative means the sector is moving away from the index rather than with it. A sector that is both outperforming and de-correlating is the shape that suggests money is being allocated to it rather than the whole market rising together. Energy leads for the fifth time in seven weeks, but with corr_shift now positive it is rising with the index rather than away from it.

subind.note: Strongest row in the universe and the only one with a rising four-week reading among the leaders. +18.9% over its 50-day but only +6.7% over its 200-day, so the move is recent. Implied vol 37.60 at the 32nd percentile with IV/HV 1.03 — implied and realised level with each other.
Silver miners. +26.39 → +19.04, decelerating for a second week without rolling over. RS_1wk is flat at +0.04. The metal itself carries IV/HV 1.08 — implied vol above realised.

+26.06 → +18.07, a second week of deceleration, with RS_1wk now negative. Positive relative strength with de-correlation for a sixth week. IV 43.39 at the 58th percentile with IV/HV 0.88 — implied below realised on a percentile that is not low.
Oil and gas E&P, the strongest energy row and +20.4% over its 200-day. corr_shift has turned positive, so it no longer qualifies on the de-correlation leg despite the relative strength.

Oil services. The only energy row still both outperforming and de-correlating. Note the split between windows: four-week +8.83 against three-month −1.34, so the trend anchor has not confirmed the recent move.
Agribusiness. Strongest one-week reading of any qualifying row at +3.23 and the largest de-correlation in the group at −0.32. Positive across all three windows.
Metals and mining, +12.84 → +7.28. Four-week positive against a three-month of −4.41: a recent move rather than an established trend.
Cloud infrastructure. Furthest above its 200-day of any row at +24.68%, with the strongest three-month anchor in technology. Correlating rather than de-correlating.
Uranium. Qualifies on both legs while sitting below its 200-day at −4.99% — outperforming from a weak base rather than extending a trend.
Biotech. Second-best three-month anchor in the universe at +22.88. corr_shift is exactly flat, so it sits on the line the screen draws.
Copper miners, +15.04 → +5.10 with RS_1wk −4.09 — the sharpest deceleration among the qualifying rows.
Software. Weakest one-week reading in the universe at −4.61 against a four-week of +4.97. The short window is a tell only, but the two disagree sharply.
Lithium. Qualifies on both legs but sits within 0.03% of its 200-day and carries a three-month of −9.69.
China internet. Furthest below its 200-day of any row at −14.18%, negative across all three windows.
RS_3mo −29.43, worst trend anchor in the universe. Included as the counterweight to the energy-strength read: the sector is not moving as a bloc.
Worst four-week reading in the universe at −11.97, and −7.3% under its 50-day. Airlines against a crude price up 21% on the month.

subNote: Sub-industry ETFs ranked by RS_4wk. A row tagged +RS · de-correlating has positive four-week relative strength against SPY and a negative correlation shift — outperforming while moving away from the index rather than with it. Thirteen of forty-four rows qualify this week against nine last week: IBIT, SIL, GDX, OIH, MOO, XME, URA, COPX, LIT, XLK, QQQ, IPO, XLB. The count rose while the leaders decelerated, which means the qualifying set broadened rather than strengthened.
volNote: IV/HV is implied vol divided by realised. Below 1.0 the market is pricing less movement than the underlying has actually been delivering; above 1.0 the reverse; around 1.0 the two are level. IV pctile ranks current implied vol against its own one-year history — note that this window changed from 13 weeks in a recent data update, so percentiles here are not comparable with those published before late August. EM is the expected move over a fixed horizon, in dollars. KRE at IV/HV 1.51 on a 7.4 percentile is the sharpest disagreement on the table: implied vol is cheap against its own year and expensive against what the underlying is actually doing.

ratios.r: Miners over metal, +13.31% in four weeks and 12.9% above the 50-day. Read both legs: GDX RS_4wk +18.07, GLD +4.18 — both positive, so the ratio is not a falling-denominator artifact. But both legs decelerated hard this week, GDX from +26.10 and GLD from +8.45, while the ratio held. The caution is unchanged: miners are equities, and this can be gold demand or it can be equity beta wearing a monetary label. The regime system's own commodities family has that flag set.

Energy equities under crude, −7.77% and 5.9% below the 50-day. Legs: XLE +9.93, USO +19.21 — both strongly positive, which is what makes this the clearest two-leg read on the page. Nothing is falling. The producers are up nearly ten points on the market and the commodity is up nineteen, and a ratio that inverted from +4.49% four weeks ago is measuring the gap, not a decline.

+14.34% → +6.01%, still 7.8% above the 50-day. Legs: IGV +4.97, SMH −0.99. Software beating semis, but on a one-week reading of −4.61 for IGV against +2.40 for SMH the short window has already turned the other way.
Silver over gold, modestly above the 50-day. Legs: SLV +6.90, GLD +4.18, both positive. Silver leading gold is normally the higher-beta expression of the same trade rather than a separate signal.
Megacap tech over semis. Legs: MAGS +1.04, SMH −0.99 — the ratio is rising mostly because the denominator is weak, not because megacap is strong. Worth separating.

Inflation-breakeven proxy, marginally above the 50-day after being below it a week ago. Legs: TIP −0.12, IEF −0.96 — both negative, so real and nominal duration are still being sold together and the ratio is measuring which is being sold harder.
Equal-weight against cap-weight, flat over four weeks and 0.9% below the 50-day. Breadth is neither confirming nor contradicting the index.

−3.53% → −8.03%, and 5.5% below the 50-day. Legs: KWEB −8.42 against FXI −0.40 — China internet losing badly to its own broad-market parent, so this is a sector problem inside China rather than a China-beta problem.

ratioNote: Every ratio is read as two legs, never as a single line. A falling ratio can mean the numerator is weak or the denominator is strong, and those are opposite conclusions. XLE/USO is this week's illustration: the ratio fell 7.77% while both legs rose.

cards.sub: 3.3rd percentile · index options near yearly cheapest

envread.sentence: Raw tally: fiscal dominance 3 votes — rates, equity internals, commodities. Currency and correlation both abstained. Effective tally is also 3, because the independence penalty applies to the rates and currency families voting together and currency did not vote. So raw equals effective for a structural reason this week, not because the evidence is independent. The system prints CONFIRMED at HIGH confidence, and there are three reasons to read that as thinner than it looks. The equity-internals family votes while failing its own independence test, at a spread of 1.77 where it needs to pass. The commodities family votes with a flag set saying the precious-metals move looks like equity beta rather than monetary demand. And the correlation family abstained on a genuine disagreement between two calibrations of the same number — the reading clears the full-history threshold and fails the trailing-ten-year one. Only the rates family is voting on unqualified evidence: a long-led steepener with derived real yields up 0.48 over twenty days. That single vote is well supported by Friday's payrolls print, which pushed the long end higher on stronger growth rather than lower. My read: the direction is right and the confidence label is doing more work than the evidence underneath it.

votes.says: Long-led steepener; derived real yields +0.48 over 20 days; 30Y 5.24% with a 20-day change of +0.37; 10Y 4.77%; 2Y 4.37% after Friday's payrolls
UUP RS_4wk +0.84 → −0.60, turning negative; 30Y 20-day change +0.37; no structural flag set
votes.vote: ABSTAIN — the dollar leg has weakened but not enough to fire

votes.says: SPY/TLT 60-day correlation 0.291 → 0.297976. Clears the full-history 95th percentile of 0.295643; sits at the 90.6th percentile of the trailing ten years, whose own threshold is 0.354191. Calibration disagreement flagged. Calibrated on 5,878 days
votes.vote: ABSTAIN — the two calibrations disagree, so it stood down

votes.says: Equal-weight/cap-weight below its 50-day; 8 of 11 sectors above their 200-day; XLP −0.83, XLV +4.05, XBI +5.82; XBI/XLV spread 1.77 fails the independence test
votes.vote: FISCAL DOMINANCE — but failing its own independence check

votes.says: GDX +18.07 against GLD +4.18, ratio +13.31%; SIL +19.04; COPX +5.10; USO RS_4wk +19.21 with RS_3mo +2.29. Gold-decoupling and miner-beta flags both set
votes.vote: FISCAL DOMINANCE · but flagged as equity beta

votes.says: High-yield OAS 265bp at 1 September against 275bp on 20 August — tightening, not widening. No stress signal
votes.vote: NO VOTE — context only, by design

votes.says: The 30-year yield is an input to both the rates and currency families, so one series would be counted twice if both voted. Currency abstained this week, so nothing was deducted
votes.vote: No penalty applied — for a structural reason

glossary.name: Fiscal dominance
glossary.plain: Government borrowing, rather than the central bank, sets the tone for interest rates. Long-term borrowing costs rise because there is a lot of government debt to sell and buyers want more compensation to hold it — not because the economy is running hot. The practical consequence, and the reason this label matters to anyone who is not a trader: government bonds stop protecting a share portfolio. In a normal downturn, bonds rise when shares fall. Under fiscal dominance they can fall together, because both are reacting to the same thing. Anyone with an ordinary superannuation or pension balance holds that mix.

glossary.name: Expansion
glossary.plain: The ordinary good state. Growth is solid, inflation is contained, and company earnings are rising. Shares generally do well, riskier assets do better than safer ones, and bonds behave the way most people expect — providing a cushion when shares fall.

glossary.name: Late cycle, hot
glossary.plain: Growth is still strong but running above what the economy can sustain. Inflation pressure builds, the central bank leans against it, and the parts of the market that do best are usually commodities and companies with pricing power rather than the fast-growing names that led earlier.

glossary.name: Stagflation
glossary.plain: The uncomfortable combination: weak growth alongside high inflation. There is no obvious hiding place, because the policies that would help one problem make the other worse. Historically it has been hard on both shares and bonds at the same time.

glossary.name: Deflationary recession
glossary.plain: Demand falls away and prices with it. Growth turns negative and inflation drops below target. This is the state in which government bonds work best — the central bank cuts rates hard, and safe assets rise while shares fall.

glossary.name: Unassigned
glossary.plain: Not a state of the world — a state of the evidence. It means the indicators disagreed enough that no single label was justified. It is deliberately preferred over naming a regime on thin agreement, and the system printed it two weeks ago.

glossaryNote: The system runs six independent families of indicators — interest rates, currencies, the correlation between shares and bonds, credit markets, share-market internals, and commodities — and each votes for a regime or abstains. A label is only assigned when enough of them agree and their evidence is genuinely independent of each other. Two families reading the same underlying number get counted once, not twice. This week the vote was three for fiscal dominance and none against, which the system marks as confirmed. Read the Environment note above before leaning on that: two of the three votes carry a failure or a flag inside them, and the missing penalty this week reflects two families abstaining rather than the evidence being independent.

macro.d: July's reported loss of 23,000 revised to a gain of 21,000. The surprise is the size of the beat, not the level. Futures moved to better than even odds of a rate hike this month; next week's CPI and PPI decide it.

Long-led bear steepener. Derived real yields +0.48 over 20 days, 30Y +0.37 over the same window. Yields were falling into Friday's payrolls print and reversed sharply on it. The 10Y touched above 4.8% intraday, a level last seen in November 2023.

macro.v: SPY implied vol 11.43 at the 3.3rd percentile
macro.d: Index options remain close to their cheapest of the past year, into a week that repriced the Fed and with the long end at multi-year highs. Implied vol sits above realised at IV/HV 1.13, so the market is pricing slightly more movement than the index has been delivering — but from a very low base.

Crude up roughly 9% on the week and 21% on the month on renewed US-Iran hostilities and disrupted transits through the Strait of Hormuz. Hormuz traffic fell to six commodity vessels on Wednesday against a ten-day average near thirteen. US diesel prices reached their highest since mid-2022. Energy equities are up but not keeping pace.

The dollar proxy has turned negative on relative strength for the first time in several weeks and sits 0.6% below its 50-day while remaining above its 200-day. Softening against a long end that keeps rising is the combination the regime system reads as fiscal dominance — but the currency family judged the move too small to vote on.

Against 275bp on 20 August and 284bp in late July. Spreads are tightening, not widening. This is not stress, and it is not a risk-on confirmation either — it is credit declining to corroborate anything the equity or rates picture is saying.

checklist: Credit spreads (high yield) starting to widen
Energy equities de-coupling from a firm oil price
checklistNote: Four conditions being watched as a late-cycle handoff. Item four ticks this week for the first time. The oil price is firm — up 9% on the week, 21% on the month — and energy equities are visibly failing to keep pace, with XLE/USO down 7.77% over four weeks and below its 50-day. Last week the condition did not cleanly apply because the crude leg was not firm; this week it is. Item one is moving the other way, with high-yield spreads tightening.
method: Sector and sub-industry ETFs are ranked weekly on relative strength against SPY over three windows — 1 week as a tell only, 4 weeks as the actionable leg, 3 months as the trend anchor — alongside a correlation shift (20-day minus 60-day) that measures whether a group is moving away from the index or with it. Ratio pairs are always read as two legs. Implied vol is compared to realised to judge whether options are pricing more or less movement than the underlying has been delivering. The regime panel is a separate voting system across six indicator families and is treated as context, never as an instruction. Everything is close-basis; nothing here is an intraday read.
disclaimer: Written for interest, not as advice. No positions, sizing or account information appears on this page, and nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell anything. Numbers are as of the US close on the stated Friday and go stale quickly.
